prompt:
57-year-old paraplegic patient with a persistent sacral ulcer and ischial osteomyelitis who underwent a diverting colostomy but has never had a colonoscopy. He takes gabapentin 300 mg TID for neuropathic pain. He has a normocytic anemia with hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL (previously 10.7-11.1), MCV 85.7 fL (stable for 2 years), reticulocyte count 1.92% (absolute 78.7 K), ferritin 1,634 ng/mL, transferrin saturation 17%, TIBC of 152 ug/dL, creatinine 1.33-1.62 mg/dL (eGFR 43-56 mL/min), BUN 41-67 mg/dL, and vitamin B12 771 pg/mL, unremarkable SPEP. He received FFP perioperatively but no red cell transfusions. What is the cause of the patient's anemia?

Provide a comprehensive management plan including appropriate diagnostic workup, referrals, procedures if indicated, follow-up, and actions to avoid.

rubric_items.text: Diagnose anemia of chronic inflammation due to the persistent pressure ulcer and chronic osteomyelitis.
Recognize stage 3 chronic kidney disease as an additional contributor to the anemia.
Interpret the elevated ferritin, low TIBC, and low transferrin saturation as inflammation-mediated iron sequestration rather than absolute iron deficiency.
Order CRP and ESR to quantify the inflammatory burden.
Calculate the corrected reticulocyte production index to confirm a hypoproliferative response.
Review a peripheral blood smear for an alternative hematologic process.
Repeat the CBC after treatment of the osteomyelitis and pressure ulcer to reassess the anemia.
Continue monitoring creatinine and eGFR for progression of chronic kidney disease.
Order urinalysis with microscopy as part of the kidney disease evaluation.
Order a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio.
Order TSH to exclude hypothyroidism as an additional contributor.
Review colorectal cancer screening history and arrange age-appropriate screening if not up to date; colonoscopy is a reasonable option, coordinated with gastroenterology given the colostomy.
Refer to infectious disease for management of chronic ischial osteomyelitis.
Refer to plastic surgery or a specialized wound service for definitive pressure-ulcer source control.
Implement consistent pressure offloading to promote ulcer healing.
Refer to a dietitian for nutritional optimization to support wound healing.
Avoid erythropoiesis-stimulating agent therapy at the current hemoglobin level.
Withhold red blood cell transfusion while the patient remains hemodynamically stable without severe anemia symptoms.
Counsel the patient about symptoms of worsening anemia that require urgent evaluation.
Refer to nephrology for chronic kidney disease evaluation and longitudinal management.
Refer to hematology if the anemia worsens, becomes otherwise unexplained, or fails to improve after inflammatory source control.

Obtain MRI of the pelvis covering the involved ischium and sacral ulcer when updated anatomic assessment is needed for operative planning or suspected complications, rather than routinely repeating imaging.
Initiate intravenous iron repletion despite the markedly elevated ferritin.
Prescribe empiric oral iron supplementation.
Transfuse packed red blood cells for the current stable hemoglobin of 10.3 g/dL.
Order a bone marrow biopsy as the initial anemia evaluation.
Prescribe vitamin B12 supplementation despite a normal vitamin B12 level.
Order capsule endoscopy for occult gastrointestinal bleeding without evidence of iron deficiency or overt bleeding.
Order CT angiography to search for a gastrointestinal bleeding source without active bleeding.
Discontinue gabapentin as treatment for the anemia.
Order whole-body PET/CT to search for occult malignancy solely because of the anemia.
Start systemic high-dose corticosteroids to treat the anemia of chronic inflammation.
Initiate therapeutic phlebotomy for presumed iron overload based only on the elevated ferritin.
Administer fresh frozen plasma to treat the anemia.
Order HFE genetic testing for hereditary hemochromatosis based only on the elevated ferritin.
Reassure the patient that colorectal cancer screening is unnecessary.
Prescribe anticoagulation as treatment for the anemia.
Order a serum erythropoietin level as part of the routine initial evaluation.
